messages.subject: (anonymised) Use BioGeoBEARS in large phylogeny
parts:
Advice on an anonymised question:

On Fri, Oct 19, 2018 at 2:41 AM XXXX wrote:
Dear Nicholas J. Matzke,

I am a researcher focusing on the macro-evolutionary patterns in some animals. I am now trying to use the BioGeoBEARS package to infer the ancestral distribution of lizards. My phylogeny is a time-tree with 4858 taxa, and the current distribution states of each tip are mapped to 20 regions (max region size = 15), so my GeoData is a 4858*20 matrix. When I test the simplest model (DEC), the calculation crashes immediately. I monitor the system usage, but fail to find any exhausted sources (CPU or memory). I guess it is caused by the large phylogeny, but even the "force_sparse = TRUE" dose not help. 

So do you have any idea in this situation? Can I cut the tree into many subtrees with smaller size and achieve the calculations in subtrees first and then try to reconstruct the ancestral states using the pruned stem tree using the results of subtrees as "current states"? 

Thanks and best wishes,
XXXXXX


Dear XXX,

Thank you for writing!  I know the cause of this issue.  It is actually not the size of your phylogeny -- it is the size of your state space.  In biogeographical models, we have a very large number of states, even if we have only 20 areas.  This is because we have every combination of presence/absence as a state.

So, if you have 3 areas, A B C, you have 8 states:

_, A, B, C, AB, AC, BC, ABC

8 states = 2^3

If you have 20 areas, you have 1048576 states, and the transition matrix (Q) is 1048576 x 1048576.  The largest transition matrix I've every seen run was only 2500x2500, and that was very slow.

If you set max_range_size to 15, you still have:

numstates_from_numareas(numareas=20, maxareas=15, include_null_range=TRUE)
[1] 1042380

...1042380 states, which is almost as huge.  

Basically, your only hope in BioGeoBEARS is to merge some areas, or lower the max areas to 3 or lower.  Use the numstates_from_numareas function:

> numstates_from_numareas(numareas=20, maxareas=4, include_null_range=TRUE)
[1] 6196
> numstates_from_numareas(numareas=20, maxareas=3, include_null_range=TRUE)
[1] 1351
> numstates_from_numareas(numareas=20, maxareas=2, include_null_range=TRUE)
[1] 211
> numstates_from_numareas(numareas=20, maxareas=1, include_null_range=TRUE)
[1] 21
> numstates_from_numareas(numareas=20, maxareas=1, include_null_range=FALSE)
[1] 20


However, you probably have observed some species occupying 15 areas, so this means you instead have to merge some of those areas.

This is a common problem, here is some saved advice:

Question: Too many areas / too many states / BioGeoBEARS too slow. Answers: diverse
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#too_many_areas

=============
So, your only choices are:

1. Reduce areas or max number of areas. Focus on what you think are the "most discrete" features in the geography, i.e. geographical features that are clearly conserved on the phylogeny. IMHO there isn't a huge point in doing ancestral state inference except on things that are pretty conserved on the phylogeny anyway.

1a. One option is to just model the centroid point of each species, thus each species occupies 1 area. You could do up to 1000 or 2000 areas this way, but you are sacrificing whatever is useful about modeling species as widespread (e.g., information about the cladogenetic process). Whether this is important depends on how likely you think it is you will successfully get such information anyway…

2. Use BayArea (the C++ program, not the BAYAREALIKE model in BioGeoBEARS). This means you are assuming BayArea's cladogenesis model (ancestral range always copied exact to both descendants, e.g. assuming widespread sympatry). RevBayes can combine BayArea-type Bayesian history sampling with cladogenesis models, but my understanding is that sampling cladogenetic histories effectively is very difficult, at least for larger problems.

3. Get sparse matrix exponentiation working in BioGeoBEARS or your own program (I can probably get sparse matrix stuff working, it would take me about a solid week which I won't have for awhile. And it might not solve your scale of problem anyway).

4. Be a genius and solve the computational problems in some new way.

5. One option is subdividing the problem into subregions and doing each separately.
=============

The one update I would make is that RevBayes now can do what the old BayArea program did -- but I don't think they've got cladogenesis models working for that large-number-of-areas problem, so you are stuck with "ranges are copied exactly at cladogenesis", i.e. no vicariance, no jump dispersal etc. The BayArea assumptions are diagrammed here (compared to other models):

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#BioGeoBEARS_supermodel_graphic


Advice on choosing meaningful areas:

How to decide your geographic areas
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#how_geog_areas

Cheers,
Nick

PS: See the BioGeoBEARS Google Group about recent code updates, I'm pasting it here if you can't access the Google Group:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/biogeobears/VHOVNUNuHOE
===================
Hi BioGeoBEARS users,

In recent years, I posted patches and updates to the BioGeoBEARS to the PhyloWiki page, and included source() commands in the example script at http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#script to source these updates. 

This was convenient as I could just keep the code on Dropbox on my various computers, and code changes would auto-update to all of my machines automatically as I traveled extensively.  It also it meant I could post quick fixes without going through CRAN. CRAN updates were challenging for BioGeoBEARS, because BioGeoBEARS relies on packages rexpokit (which wraps FORTRAN code used by BioGeoBEARS to make calculations run faster) and cladoRcpp (which wraps C++ code). 

CRAN packages are very useful, because CRAN produces binary install files that install easily on Windows, Macs, and other machines, without the need for downloading compilers and setting compiler options, which can be a real nightmare e.g. when teaching a workshop to students with diverse computers and computational backgrounds. However, updating CRAN packages that contain FORTRAN or C++ can be very challenging, because CRAN keeps changing its standards as compilers and compiler flags change, and many of the warnings/notes that result have very obscure causes. Over the years, this meant that rexpokit and cladoRcpp accumulated more and more warnings/notes etc. on in CRAN's "R CMD check" function, and it became a very big project to dig back into the arcane details needed to fix up the FORTRAN/C++ source code to pass R CMD check.

Anyway: I have finally gotten around to doing it, so there are now new versions of rexpokit and cladoRcpp on CRAN, and CRAN has also now generated binaries for these. So, everyone should update these packages, with these commands:

# 1. Install the new rexpokit, version 0.26.6 from CRAN:
install.packages('rexpokit')

# 2. Install the new cladoRcpp version 0.15 from CRAN:
install.packages('cladoRcpp')

With these packages installed, all of the BioGeoBEARS updates can be installed from GitHub, rather than re-running the source() commands again and again. This version is being called BioGeoBEARS v1.1, and should be referenced as such. Once BioGeoBEARS is installed from GitHub, you do not have to re-install it again until you want to, and you should delete all of the source() commands that we were using previously.

# 3. Install devtools from CRAN:
install.packages('devtools')

# 4. Install the updated BioGeoBEARS from GitHub, install with:
library(devtools)
devtools::install_github(repo='nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS')

# 5. Finally, run library() on these packages:
library(rexpokit)
library(cladoRcpp)
library(BioGeoBEARS)

The code updates include the code for Biogeographic Stochastic Mapping, trait-dependent dispersal, etc., previously mentioned on PhyloWiki. 

I am working on getting the updated BioGeoBEARS onto CRAN -- including updated help files/documentation, and using CRAN's updated system for linking functions etc. -- but this is less of a priority, as BioGeoBEARS itself is "pure R" and so installs easily from GitHub without any messing around from compilers.

EXPECTED WARNINGS: When you install from GitHub, you will get various warnings about e.g. function linking and the lack of man/help files, but you can ignore these for now.

HELP: If you need help for functions, use Google to find the old help/man pages on CRAN, or search the BioGeoBEARS Google Group. 

I will update the various PhyloWiki scripts to remove the source() commands when I get a chance. If run, the source() commands will now all pop up a message giving the above information about the updates and where to find them. 


Citation information: A permalink for Version 1.1 is available as a DOI:

Matzke, Nicholas J. (2018). BioGeoBEARS: BioGeography with Bayesian (and likelihood) Evolutionary Analysis with R Scripts. version 1.1, published on GitHub on October 10, 2018. DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1463216  GitHub: https://github.com/nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS

Please let me know if you have any problems / installation failures (not just warnings).

Cheers!
Nick Matzke
